date.note: Published in German as Ich und Du (Leipzig: Insel Verlag, 1923). English translations by Ronald Gregor Smith (1937, as I and Thou) and Walter Kaufmann (1970, rendering the pair as I-You).

summary: I and Thou (Ich und Du, 1923) is Martin Buber's founding statement of his philosophy of dialogue. It distinguishes two basic ways a person stands toward the world, named by the word pairs I-Thou (Ich-Du), the mutual, present, whole encounter with another, and I-It (Ich-Es), the relation of experience and use, and it holds that the extended lines of every I-Thou relation meet in the Eternal Thou (das ewige Du), God, who on Buber's account can never be made into an It.
description:
Ich und Du, published by Insel Verlag in Leipzig in 1923 and known in English as I and Thou, is the founding statement of Martin Buber's philosophy of dialogue and his most widely read book. Its argument is organized around two 'basic words' (Grundworte), which are word pairs: I-Thou (Ich-Du) and I-It (Ich-Es). In the I-It attitude a person experiences and uses things, holding them at a distance as objects of knowledge and utility; in the I-Thou attitude a person enters a mutual, present, and whole relation with another, an address and response in which the other is met as a partner rather than handled as an object. In Walter Kaufmann's translation, 'the basic word I-You can only be spoken with one's whole being,' whereas 'the basic word I-It can never be spoken with one's whole being,' and 'all actual life is encounter.' Buber holds that no human Thou can remain a Thou permanently: every Thou in the world is fated to become an It again, and human life moves between the two attitudes.

The book's third part turns to God as the Eternal Thou (das ewige Du). In Kaufmann's rendering, 'in each You we address the eternal You': every particular I-Thou encounter, on Buber's account, points toward the one Thou that by its nature can never become an It, and God is met not by turning away from the world but in and through the meeting with each particular Thou. Religion, on this account, lives in the immediacy of relation rather than in propositions about God, an account given here as the work's own attributed teaching.

Scholarship on the book's genesis places it within Buber's turn from mysticism to dialogue and within his collaboration with Franz Rosenzweig. Paul Mendes-Flohr's study From Mysticism to Dialogue traces the shift in Buber's thought from his early mystical writings to the dialogical philosophy the book announces. Rivka Horwitz's historical analysis showed that themes of the book took shape in the lectures 'Religion als Gegenwart' ('Religion as Presence') that Buber delivered in 1922 at the Freies Judisches Lehrhaus in Frankfurt, the house of Jewish study led by Rosenzweig, and she published those lectures together with the correspondence in which Rosenzweig read and commented on the book in draft. Buber later described Ich und Du as the first of a planned larger series of works on dialogue that he did not carry out in that form, and he continued to restate and develop its themes in later essays. The book has been read across religious and philosophical traditions, and within Jewish thought it stands with Rosenzweig's Star of Redemption among the central statements of the dialogical or 'new' thinking of the interwar German-Jewish renaissance; these placements are recorded as the scholarship's characterizations.
editorial_notes:
This entry presents I and Thou on its author's own terms as the founding statement of Buber's philosophy of dialogue (neutrality #1, #4, #6). The I-Thou / I-It distinction, the Eternal Thou, and the claim that God can never become an It are stated throughout as the work's own attributed teaching, described and not affirmed or denied by the editor. The placement of the book within the dialogical thinking of the interwar German-Jewish renaissance is attributed to the scholarship.

No high rating is claimed for any source. sources.citation: Horwitz, Rivka. Buber's Way to I and Thou: An Historical Analysis and the First Publication of Martin Buber's Lectures 'Religion als Gegenwart.' Heidelberg: Lambert Schneider, 1978 (expanded English edition: Buber's Way to 'I and Thou': The Development of Martin Buber's Thought and His 'Religion as Presence' Lectures. Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 1988). The standard historical study of the book's genesis, publishing for the first time the 1922 'Religion als Gegenwart' lectures Buber delivered at Rosenzweig's Freies Judisches Lehrhaus and documenting, from the Martin Buber Archive in Jerusalem, the development of the book's themes and the correspondence around its drafting; cited for the account of the work's genesis and the Buber-Rosenzweig exchange. Verified to exist and be on-topic (PhilPapers record; National Library of Israel record; JPS edition ISBN 0827603059), not read line-by-line.

Mendes-Flohr, Paul. From Mysticism to Dialogue: Martin Buber's Transformation of German Social Thought. Culture of Jewish Modernity. Detroit: Wayne State University Press, 1989. An academic study tracing the shift in Buber's thought from his early mysticism to the philosophy of dialogue announced in Ich und Du, situating it within German social thought; cited as the academic lens on the book's intellectual genesis and context. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Wayne State University Press; PhilPapers and library records), not read line-by-line.

Kepnes, Steven. The Text as Thou: Martin Buber's Dialogical Hermeneutics and Narrative Theology. Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1992. A contemporary Jewish scholar's study of Buber's dialogical philosophy extended into hermeneutics and narrative theology; cited as the contemporary-scholarly lens on the I-Thou relation and its reception. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Indiana University Press), not read line-by-line; carries the same medium rating it holds in the martin-buber entry.
